title: Sinusoidal Functions of the Form f(x) = a sin[k(x − d)] + c and f(x) = a cos[k(x − d)] + c
overview: Now all four transformations happen at once. You will read the amplitude, period, phase shift and vertical translation from an equation, build equations from a description or a graph, and model rides, buoys, engines and temperatures. The extension shows how technology fits a sinusoidal model to real data.
objectives: Determine the amplitude, period, phase shift and vertical translation of $f(x)=a\sin[k(x-d)]+c$ and $f(x)=a\cos[k(x-d)]+c$.
Factor the argument to find the phase shift when the equation is not in standard form.
Sketch sinusoidal functions by applying transformations to key points.
Write an equation of a sinusoidal function from its properties or its graph.
Model real situations with sinusoidal functions and interpret the parameters.
Use and interpret sinusoidal regression from technology.

lessons.title: The general form and what each parameter does
lessons.body:
Every transformed sine or cosine function in this course can be written as

$$f(x)=a\sin[k(x-d)]+c\qquad\text{or}\qquad f(x)=a\cos[k(x-d)]+c$$

| Parameter | Job | How to read it |
|---|---|---|
| $a$ | vertical stretch; reflection if $a<0$ | amplitude $=\lvert a\rvert$ |
| $k$ | horizontal stretch/compression | period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lvert k\rvert}$ |
| $d$ | horizontal translation (phase shift) | right if $d>0$, left if $d<0$ |
| $c$ | vertical translation | midline $y=c$; max $=c+\lvert a\rvert$, min $=c-\lvert a\rvert$ |


```plot
title: y = 2.5 sin[π(x + 1)] + 1.5 compared with y = sin x
f: 2.5*sin(pi*(x+1))+1.5 | label=y = 2.5 sin[π(x+1)] + 1.5
f: sin(x) | dashed; label=y = sin x
domain: -2, 4
range: -2, 4.5
ticks: 1, 1
```


Here amplitude $2.5$, period $\frac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$, phase shift $1$ left, midline $y=1.5$, max $4$, min $-1$.

> **Order matters when sketching by hand:** apply the stretches ($a$ and $k$) first, then the translations ($d$ and $c$).

lessons.title: Factor out k before reading the phase shift
lessons.body:
Equations are not always written in the tidy form. In $g(x)=2\cos(3x+2)-5$ it is tempting to say "phase shift 2 left" – **wrong**.

Factor the coefficient of $x$ out of the bracket:
$$3x+2=3\left(x+\tfrac23\right)\quad\Rightarrow\quad g(x)=2\cos\left[3\left(x+\tfrac23\right)\right]-5$$

Now the phase shift is $\frac23$ rad **left**. The 2 was being multiplied by $\frac13$ – the same horizontal compression that affects every $x$-value.

Similarly $y=3\cos\left(2x-\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=3\cos\left[2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right]$: phase shift $\frac{\pi}{4}$ right.

lessons.title: Writing an equation from given properties
lessons.body:
A four-step recipe works for almost every problem:

1. **Amplitude:** $a=\dfrac{\max-\min}{2}$.
2. **Vertical translation:** $c=\dfrac{\max+\min}{2}$.
3. **$k$ from the period:** $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{\text{period}}$.
4. **Phase shift $d$:** find where one recognisable point of the parent ends up.
   * For **cosine**, $d$ = an $x$-value of a **maximum**.
   * For **sine**, $d$ = an $x$-value where the graph crosses the **midline going up**.
   * Or, if a sine maximum is at $x=m$: a sine max normally occurs a quarter period after its start, so $d=m-\frac{T}{4}$.

**Example (properties).** Amplitude 4, period $\pi$, phase shift $\frac{\pi}{6}$ left, up 2:
$a=4$, $k=\frac{2\pi}{\pi}=2$, $d=-\frac{\pi}{6}$, $c=2$, so $g(x)=4\cos\left[2\left(x+\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]+2$.

The same graph has **many** correct equations: you can shift by any whole number of periods, switch between sine and cosine (shift by a quarter period), or use a negative $a$ with a half-period shift.

lessons.title: Reading an equation from a graph
lessons.body:
```plot
title: Find an equation for this graph
f: 3*cos(2*(x-pi/4))+1
domain: -pi/2, 2*pi
range: -3, 5
xticks: pi
points: (pi/4,4), (3*pi/4,-2), (5*pi/4,4)
```


* Max $=4$, min $=-2$ → $a=\frac{4-(-2)}{2}=3$, $c=\frac{4+(-2)}{2}=1$.
* Consecutive maxima at $\frac{\pi}{4}$ and $\frac{5\pi}{4}$ → period $\pi$ → $k=2$.
* A maximum at $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$ → for cosine, $d=\frac{\pi}{4}$.

$$y=3\cos\left[2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{4}\right)\right]+1$$

As a sine function, the graph crosses the midline going up a quarter period ($\frac{\pi}{4}$) before the max, at $x=0$: $y=3\sin2x+1$. Both are correct – check by substituting a point.

lessons.title: Modelling rides, waves and engines
lessons.body:
Real problems give you the four ingredients in words.

**The Round-Up ride.** Max height 7.5 m, min 1.5 m, one turn every 5 s, highest point at $t=0$.

* $a=\frac{7.5-1.5}{2}=3$, $c=\frac{7.5+1.5}{2}=4.5$, $k=\frac{2\pi}{5}=0.4\pi$.
* Cosine is easiest because cosine starts at a maximum: $h=3\cos(0.4\pi t)+4.5$.
* With sine, a maximum normally occurs at $\frac14$ of a period ($1.25$ s); we need it at $t=0$, so shift **left** $1.25$: $h=3\sin[0.4\pi(t+1.25)]+4.5$.


```plot
title: Round-Up height h(t)
f: 3*cos(0.4*pi*x)+4.5 | label=h = 3 cos(0.4πt) + 4.5
domain: 0, 10
range: 0, 8
ticks: 1, 1
points: (0,7.5), (2.5,1.5), (5,7.5)
```


**Units of $k$.** If $t$ is in seconds and the period is $T$ seconds, $k=\frac{2\pi}{T}$ has units of radians per second. If an engine turns at 2100 rpm, the period is $\frac{60}{2100}$ s.

**Starting conditions.** Read carefully whether the object starts at the top, the bottom, or the middle (going up or down):

| Starts at… | Simplest model |
|---|---|
| maximum | $a\cos kt+c$ |
| minimum | $-a\cos kt+c$ |
| midline, going up | $a\sin kt+c$ |
| midline, going down | $-a\sin kt+c$ |

lessons.title: Extension: sinusoidal regression with technology
lessons.body:
When you have real data (temperatures, tides, daylight), a graphing calculator's **SinReg** (or software such as Desmos) finds the sinusoidal function that best fits the points. It usually reports the form
$$y=a\sin(bx+c)+d$$
which you can rewrite in our form by factoring: $a\sin\left[b\left(x+\frac{c}{b}\right)\right]+d$ – so the phase shift is $-\frac{c}{b}$.

Good habits:
* **Build your own model first** from the max, min and period, then compare with the regression. The values should be close.
* Enter at least one full cycle of data; regression with less than a cycle can give misleading periods.
* Look at the **residuals** (how far points are from the curve) to judge the fit, and think about why real data are not perfectly sinusoidal.

keyTerms.definition: A function of the form $f(x)=a\sin[k(x-d)]+c$ or $f(x)=a\cos[k(x-d)]+c$.
The horizontal line $y=c$ halfway between the maximum and minimum.
The horizontal translation $d$, read only after factoring $k$ out of the argument.
A statistical process, usually done with technology, that finds the sinusoidal function that best fits a set of data.
One complete repetition of the pattern of a periodic function.

formulas.name: Amplitude and vertical translation

workedExamples.title: Transform a cosine function
workedExamples.problem: Transform $f(x)=\cos x$ into $g(x)$ with amplitude 4, period $\pi$, phase shift $\frac{\pi}{6}$ left and vertical translation 2 up. Describe two cycles.
steps:
Maxima ($y=6$) at $x=-\frac{\pi}{6},\ \frac{5\pi}{6},\ \frac{11\pi}{6}$; minima ($y=-2$) at $x=\frac{\pi}{3},\ \frac{4\pi}{3}$.

```plot
f: 4*cos(2*(x+pi/6))+2
f: 4*cos(2*x) | dashed
domain: -pi/2, 2*pi
range: -3, 7
xticks: pi
```

workedExamples.title: Data not in terms of π
workedExamples.problem: Transform $f(x)=\sin x$ to have amplitude 2, period 1, phase shift 0.5 left and vertical translation 3 up.
steps:
The period is 1, so the graph completes one cycle every 1 unit; max 5, min 1.

```plot
f: 2*sin(2*pi*(x+0.5))+3
domain: -1, 2
range: 0, 6
ticks: 0.25, 1
```

workedExamples.title: Reading a messy equation
workedExamples.problem: State the amplitude, period, phase shift and vertical translation of $y=-2\cos\left[4\left(x+\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)\right]-3$, and its maximum and minimum.
steps: Vertical translation 3 down: midline $y=-3$, max $-1$, min $-5$.

workedExamples.title: Buoy on a lake
workedExamples.problem: A buoy bobs so that the distance between its highest and lowest points is 1.5 m, completing a cycle every 6 s. At $t=0$ it is at equilibrium and moving down. Model its vertical displacement $v$.
steps: Starts at the midline going **down**: use $-a\sin kt$.

workedExamples.title: Aircraft piston
workedExamples.problem: A piston moves between 25 cm and 75 cm from the crankshaft at 2100 rpm. Model its position $h$ (cm) at time $t$ (s), starting at the maximum.

misconceptions.myth: In $y=\cos(3x+2)$ the phase shift is 2 to the left.
misconceptions.fact: Factor first: $\cos[3(x+\frac23)]$. The phase shift is $\frac23$ left.

misconceptions.myth: The vertical translation is the minimum value.
misconceptions.fact: The vertical translation is the **midline**, halfway between max and min: $c=\frac{\max+\min}{2}$.

misconceptions.myth: Amplitude is the distance from max to min.
misconceptions.fact: That distance is **twice** the amplitude. Amplitude $=\frac{\max-\min}{2}$.

misconceptions.myth: There is only one correct equation for a sinusoidal graph.
misconceptions.fact: Infinitely many: shift by whole periods, switch sine/cosine with a quarter-period shift, or reflect and shift a half period.
$k$ is the number of cycles per $2\pi$; the period is $\frac{2\pi}{k}$.

realWorld.title: Breathing
realWorld.body: The volume of air in your lungs during normal breathing can be modelled by $V=a\sin[k(t-d)]+c$: $a$ is half the volume of one breath, $c$ includes the air that always stays in your lungs, and the period is the time for one breath.

realWorld.title: Ferris wheels
realWorld.body: The height of a gondola on a wheel of radius $r$ whose hub is $c$ m above the ground is $h=r\sin[k(t-d)]+c$, with $k=\frac{2\pi}{\text{time per revolution}}$.

realWorld.title: Gravitron ride
realWorld.body: A rider on a ride of radius 4 m and period 2 s has position $x=4\sin(\pi t)$, $y=4\cos(\pi t)$, and $x^2+y^2=16$ for every $t$ – the rider stays on the circle.

realWorld.title: Moon illumination
realWorld.body: The fraction of the Moon that is lit follows a roughly sinusoidal pattern with a period of about 29.5 days.

practice.question: Determine the amplitude and period of $y=-3\cos\frac43x$.
For $y=4\sin\left[3\left(x-\frac{\pi}{3}\right)\right]+2$ state the amplitude, period, phase shift and vertical translation.
A sine function has max 7, min $-1$, phase shift $\frac{3\pi}{4}$ left and period $\frac{\pi}{2}$. Write its equation.
A cosine function has max 1, min $-5$, phase shift 2 rad right and period 3. Write its equation.
Explain why $g(x)=3\sin\left[2\left(x+\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\right]+4$ has no zeros.
practice.solution: Min $=c-|a|=4-3=1>0$, so the graph never reaches the $x$-axis.

practice.question: Model the Round-Up ride (max 7.5 m, min 1.5 m, period 5 s, highest at $t=0$) using a cosine function.
A Ferris wheel gondola follows $h=10\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{15}(t-d)\right]+12$. Find a phase shift so that $h=7$ m at $t=0$ while rising.
practice.solution: $\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{15}d\right)=-0.5$. For the gondola to be rising, the argument must lie on the increasing part of the sine curve, so $-\frac{\pi}{15}d=-\frac{\pi}{6}$ and $d=2.5$. Model: $h=10\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{15}(t-2.5)\right]+12$. Check: $h(0)=10\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12=7$ ✓.

summary: $f(x)=a\sin[k(x-d)]+c$: amplitude $|a|$, period $\frac{2\pi}{k}$, phase shift $d$, vertical translation $c$.
Always factor $k$ out of the argument before reading the phase shift.
Cosine models start at a max; sine models start on the midline going up.
A graph has many equivalent equations; check by substituting a point.
Sinusoidal regression fits a model to data; compare it with a model built by hand.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Amplitude $={{a}}$.

(b) Period $=\dfrac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }\approx{{2*pi/k:3}}$.

(c) Phase shift $\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ to the right.

(d) Vertical translation {{c}} units up; midline $y={{c}}$.

(e) Max $={{c}}+{{a}}={{c+a}}$; min $={{c}}-{{a}}={{c-a}}$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: What is the amplitude? What does the negative sign do?

parts.label: b
parts.text: What is the period?

parts.label: c
parts.text: Describe the phase shift.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe the vertical translation and state the range.

parts.label: e
parts.text: Is there a maximum or a minimum at $x=-\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Amplitude $\lvert-{{a}}\rvert={{a}}$; the negative sign reflects the graph in the $x$-axis.

(b) Period $=\frac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }\approx{{2*pi/k:3}}$.

(c) Phase shift $\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ to the left.

(d) Vertical translation {{c}} down; midline $y=-{{c}}$; range $-{{c+a}}\le y\le {{a-c}}$.

(e) Because of the reflection, the graph has a **minimum** (not a maximum) at $x=-\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$.

rubric.point: Identifies minimum at the phase shift due to reflection

questions.text: Consider $g(x)={{a}}\cos({{k}}x+{{b}})-{{c}}$. A student says the phase shift is {{b}} rad to the left. Explain the error and determine the actual phase shift, amplitude, period and vertical translation.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phase shift (rad, left)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Period

questions.modelAnswer:
The phase shift is only read directly when the coefficient of $x$ inside the bracket is 1. Factor {{k}} out:
$${{k}}x+{{b}}={{k}}\left(x+\frac{ {{b}} }{ {{k}} }\right)$$
so $g(x)={{a}}\cos\left[{{k}}\left(x+{{b/k:3}}\right)\right]-{{c}}$.

Phase shift $\frac{ {{b}} }{ {{k}} }\approx{{b/k:3}}$ rad **left**; amplitude {{a}}; period $\frac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }\approx{{2*pi/k:3}}$; vertical translation {{c}} down.

questions.text: A sine function has a maximum value of {{mx}}, a minimum value of {{mn}}, a phase shift of $\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ rad to the left, and a period of $\frac{\pi}{ {{p}} }$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine $a$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine $c$.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine $k$.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Write the equation and verify that it has the given properties.

questions.modelAnswer:
$a=\dfrac{ {{mx}}-({{mn}}) }{2}={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}$, $c=\dfrac{ {{mx}}+({{mn}}) }{2}={{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$.

$k=\dfrac{2\pi}{\pi/{{p}}}={{2*p}}$, $d=-\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$.

$$y={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}\sin\left[{{2*p}}\left(x+\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }\right)\right]+{{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$$

Check: max $={{(mx+mn)/2:3}}+{{(mx-mn)/2:3}}={{mx}}$ ✓; one cycle has length $\frac{\pi}{ {{p}} }$ ✓; the cycle starts (midline, rising) at $x=-\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ ✓.

questions.text: A cosine function has a maximum value of {{mx}}, a minimum value of {{mn}}, a phase shift of {{d}} rad to the right, and a period of {{T}}.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine $k$.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the equation and verify it.

questions.text:
Model the graph shown using a **cosine** function.

```plot
f: {{a}}*cos({{k}}*(x-pi/{{n}}))+{{c}}
domain: -pi, 2*pi
xticks: pi
points: (pi/{{n}}, {{a+c}})
```

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the amplitude, vertical translation, period and phase shift.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write an equation.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Verify your equation using two points on the graph.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) From the graph: max $={{a+c}}$, min $={{c-a}}$, so amplitude $={{a}}$ and vertical translation $={{c}}$. Consecutive maxima are $\frac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }$ apart, so the period is $\frac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }$. A maximum occurs at $x=\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$, so the phase shift is $\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$ right.

(b) $y={{a}}\cos\left[{{k}}\left(x-\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }\right)\right]+{{c}}$.

(c) Verify: at $x=\frac{\pi}{ {{n}} }$, $y={{a}}\cos0+{{c}}={{a+c}}$ ✓; half a period later the graph is at its minimum {{c-a}} ✓.

rubric.point: Correct amplitude and vertical translation from the graph

questions.text:
Model the graph shown using a **sine** function, then give a second, different equation for the same graph.

```plot
f: {{a}}*sin({{k}}*(x-{{d}}))+{{c}}
domain: -2, 6
ticks: 1, 1
points: ({{d}}, {{c}})
```
questions.modelAnswer:
Max $={{a+c}}$, min $={{c-a}}$: $a={{a}}$, $c={{c}}$.

The graph crosses its midline going up at $x={{d}}$, and its period is about {{2*pi/k:3}}, so $k=\frac{2\pi}{\text{period}}={{k}}$.

Equation 1: $y={{a}}\sin[{{k}}(x-{{d}})]+{{c}}$.

Equation 2 (one of many): shift by one full period, $y={{a}}\sin\left[{{k}}\left(x-{{d}}-\frac{2\pi}{ {{k}} }\right)\right]+{{c}}$, or use cosine with the maximum a quarter period later: $y={{a}}\cos\left[{{k}}\left(x-{{d}}-\frac{\pi}{2({{k}})}\right)\right]+{{c}}$.

rubric.point: Phase shift from rising midline crossing

questions.text: The maximum height of a theme-park ride is {{mx}} m and its minimum is {{mn}} m. It completes one rotation every {{T}} s and is at its highest point at $t=0$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a cosine model for the height $h$ (m) after $t$ s.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write a sine model.

parts.label: c
parts.text: When does the rider first reach the lowest point, and how high is it?

questions.modelAnswer:
$a=\frac{ {{mx}}-{{mn}} }{2}={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}$; $c=\frac{ {{mx}}+{{mn}} }{2}={{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$; $k=\frac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }\approx{{2*pi/T:3}}$.

(a) Cosine starts at a maximum: $h={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }t\right)+{{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$.

(b) A sine maximum normally occurs $\frac{T}{4}={{T/4:3}}$ s after its start; to have it at $t=0$, shift **left** {{T/4:3}} s: $h={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}\sin\left[\frac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }(t+{{T/4:3}})\right]+{{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$.

(c) At $t=\frac{T}{2}={{T/2:3}}$ s, the rider is at the minimum height {{mn}} m.

rubric.point: Correct sine model with quarter-period shift

questions.text: A buoy bobs up and down. The distance between its highest and lowest points is {{H}} m and it takes {{T}} s to complete a cycle. At $t=0$ it is at its equilibrium point and moving **down**.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Model the vertical displacement $v$ (m) at time $t$ (s).

parts.label: b
parts.text: When is the buoy first at its lowest point?

parts.label: c
parts.text: When is it first at its highest point?

questions.modelAnswer:
Amplitude $=\frac{ {{H}} }{2}={{H/2:3}}$ m; midline $v=0$; $k=\frac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }\approx{{2*pi/T:3}}$.

Starting at the midline and going down means a reflected sine: $v=-{{H/2:3}}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }t\right)$.

The buoy is lowest a quarter period later, at $t={{T/4:3}}$ s, and highest at $t={{3*T/4:3}}$ s.

rubric.point: Uses −sin to match start going down
Correct times of lowest and highest points

questions.text: A piston in an engine moves horizontally between a minimum distance of {{mn}} cm and a maximum of {{mx}} cm from the crankshaft at {{rpm}} rpm. At $t=0$ it is at its maximum distance.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the period.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write the model.

parts.label: c
parts.text: What changes to the model if the engine speed increases? Explain.

questions.modelAnswer:
$a=\frac{ {{mx}}-{{mn}} }{2}={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}$, $c=\frac{ {{mx}}+{{mn}} }{2}={{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$.

Period: $\frac{60}{ {{rpm}} }\approx{{60/rpm:3}}$ s, so $k=2\pi\cdot\frac{ {{rpm}} }{60}={{rpm/30:4}}\pi$.

$h={{(mx-mn)/2:3}}\cos({{rpm/30:4}}\pi t)+{{(mx+mn)/2:3}}$.

If the engine speed increases, only $k$ changes (period shorter); amplitude and midline stay the same because the piston still travels between the same positions.

questions.text: A Ferris wheel gondola's height is $h=10\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{15}(t-d)\right]+12$, where $t$ is in seconds. The gondola must be at a height of {{h0}} m at $t=0$ and moving upward.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Determine the required phase shift $d$ (in seconds).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Show that your answer is correct and describe a different method.

questions.modelAnswer:
At $t=0$: $10\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{15}d\right)+12={{h0}}$, so $\sin\left(-\frac{\pi}{15}d\right)={{(h0-12)/10:3}}$.

For the gondola to be rising, the argument must be on the increasing part of the sine curve (between $-\frac{\pi}{2}$ and $\frac{\pi}{2}$), so $-\frac{\pi}{15}d=\sin^{-1}({{(h0-12)/10:3}})\approx{{asin((h0-12)/10):4}}$.

$d=-\frac{15}{\pi}({{asin((h0-12)/10):4}})\approx{{-15/pi*asin((h0-12)/10):3}}$ s.

Check: $h(0)=10\sin({{asin((h0-12)/10):4}})+12\approx{{h0}}$ ✓, and a slightly larger $t$ gives a larger height ✓. (Another method: find the time after the rising midline crossing at which $h={{h0}}$ on the graph.)

rubric.point: Chooses the rising branch with justification

questions.text: (a) Explain why $g(x)={{a}}\sin\left[2\left(x+\frac{3\pi}{4}\right)\right]+{{c}}$ has no zeros. (b) Without graphing, decide whether $h(x)={{a}}\cos x+{{c2}}$ has zeros, and justify.
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) The minimum of $g$ is $c-|a|={{c}}-{{a}}={{c-a}}>0$, so the whole graph lies above the $x$-axis and never crosses it.

(b) Min of $h$ is ${{c2}}-{{a}}={{c2-a}}$ and max is ${{c2+a}}$. Since the minimum is negative and the maximum positive, the graph must cross the $x$-axis: $h$ has zeros (two in each period).

rubric.point: Uses minimum value to explain no zeros

questions.text: A Gravitron ride has radius {{r}} m and period {{T}} s, with the origin at the centre of rotation. A rider starts at the point $(0,{{r}})$.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Model the $x$-position using a sine function.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Model the $y$-position using a cosine function.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Show that $x^2+y^2$ is constant and find its value.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Explain why this must be true.

questions.modelAnswer:
$k=\frac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }$.

(a) $x={{r}}\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }t\right)$ (starts at 0, increases).

(b) $y={{r}}\cos\left(\frac{2\pi}{ {{T}} }t\right)$ (starts at the maximum {{r}}).

(c) $x^2+y^2={{r}}^2\left[\sin^2\left(\tfrac{2\pi t}{ {{T}} }\right)+\cos^2\left(\tfrac{2\pi t}{ {{T}} }\right)\right]={{r}}^2(1)={{r*r}}$.

(d) This is the equation of a circle of radius {{r}}: the rider is always {{r}} m from the centre, which is exactly what a rotating ride does.

rubric.point: Shows x² + y² = r² using the Pythagorean identity

questions.text: A sine function is transformed so that it has a single $x$-intercept in the interval $[0,\pi)$, a period of $\pi$, and a $y$-intercept of {{y0}}. (a) Determine an equation that satisfies these properties. (b) Verify each property. (c) Are there other sine functions with these properties? Give one or explain why not.
questions.modelAnswer:
Period $\pi$ gives $k=2$. A single $x$-intercept per period means the graph just touches the $x$-axis at its minimum, so $c=|a|$. With no phase shift, the $y$-intercept is $c$ (since $\sin0=0$), so $c={{y0}}$ and $a={{y0}}$:

$$y={{y0}}\sin2x+{{y0}}$$

Check: min $=0$ (touches the axis once, at $x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$), period $\pi$, $y(0)={{y0}}$ ✓.

Other answers exist, e.g. $y=-{{y0}}\sin2x+{{y0}}$ (touches at $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$), or functions using a phase shift together with a different $a$ and $c$ chosen to keep the $y$-intercept {{y0}}.

rubric.point: Recognises single intercept means min (or max) on the axis

parts.label: a
parts.text: Write a sinusoidal function $T(m)$ to model the data.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Comment on how well your model fits the data.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why a sinusoidal model is appropriate.

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Max $\approx{{lo+2*A}}$ (July, month 7), min $\approx{{lo}}$ (January).

$a=\frac{ {{lo+2*A}}-({{lo}}) }{2}={{A}}$; $c=\frac{ {{lo+2*A}}+({{lo}}) }{2}={{lo+A}}$; period 12 months so $k=\frac{2\pi}{12}=\frac{\pi}{6}$.

A sine maximum normally occurs at $\frac{12}{4}=3$; the data's maximum is at 7, so the phase shift is $7-3=4$ right:
$$T={{A}}\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(m-4)\right]+{{lo+A}}$$

(b) A good fit: the model passes close to most points; differences of 1–2 °C are expected because real weather is not perfectly sinusoidal.

(c) Seasonal temperature repeats every year between a high and a low, so a periodic sinusoidal model is appropriate.

rubric.point: Correct amplitude and midline from data

questions.text: A graphing calculator's sinusoidal regression for some data returns $y={{a}}\sin({{b}}x+{{cc}})+{{dd}}$. (a) Rewrite the equation in the form $y=a\sin[k(x-d)]+c$. (b) State the amplitude, period, phase shift and vertical translation. (c) Explain why you should still build a model by hand from the data before using regression.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Phase shift magnitude (rad)

parts.label: b
parts.text: Period

questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Factor {{b}} out: ${{b}}x+{{cc}}={{b}}\left(x+\frac{ {{cc}} }{ {{b}} }\right)$, so $y={{a}}\sin\left[{{b}}\left(x-({{-cc/b:3}})\right)\right]+({{dd}})$.

(b) Amplitude {{a}}; period $\frac{2\pi}{ {{b}} }\approx{{2*pi/b:3}}$; phase shift $d\approx{{-cc/b:3}}$ (a positive value means right, negative means left); vertical translation {{dd}}.

(c) Building a model from the max, min and period lets you check that the regression is sensible (technology can return a strange fit, especially with less than a full cycle of data), and it shows you understand what each parameter means in context.

rubric.point: Sound reason for a hand model

questions.text: Explain, using the Round-Up example (max 7.5 m, min 1.5 m, period 5 s, highest point at $t=0$), how the **same** situation can be modelled by both a sine function and a cosine function. Write both models and explain how they are related.
questions.modelAnswer:
$a=3$, $c=4.5$, $k=\frac{2\pi}{5}=0.4\pi$.

Cosine: $h=3\cos(0.4\pi t)+4.5$, since cosine starts at a maximum.

Sine: a sine maximum normally occurs a quarter period ($1.25$ s) after the start, so shift left 1.25 s: $h=3\sin[0.4\pi(t+1.25)]+4.5$.

They are related by $\cos\theta=\sin\left(\theta+\frac{\pi}{2}\right)$: a quarter-period shift ($\frac{\pi}{2}$ in the argument, $1.25$ s in time) changes one into the other.

questions.text: Write an equation for a transformed **cosine** function that includes at least three transformations. Then write the minimum set of clues (e.g. max, min, period, a point) that would let a classmate determine your equation exactly. Show that your clues are sufficient by solving your own problem, and explain whether more than one answer is possible.
questions.modelAnswer:
Sample: $y=2\cos\left[3\left(x-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)\right]+1$.

Clues: max 3, min $-1$, period $\frac{2\pi}{3}$, a maximum at $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$.

Solve: $a=\frac{3-(-1)}{2}=2$, $c=1$, $k=\frac{2\pi}{2\pi/3}=3$, and a maximum at $\frac{\pi}{6}$ gives $d=\frac{\pi}{6}$ ✓.

More than one answer is possible: any $d=\frac{\pi}{6}+\frac{2\pi n}{3}$ gives the same graph, and the graph could also be written as a sine function. The clues determine the **graph** uniquely but not the **equation**.

rubric.point: Valid equation with three or more transformations
